title: US being left behind in EV charging speeds as China goes sub-5 min to 70%
gist: Chinese battery makers are racing to megawatt charging (Geely 2.2 MW, 10-70% in 4.5 minutes; BYD 5 minutes; CATL LFP 10-80% in 3:44), while US passenger-EV chargers top out at 250-600 kW and US EVs accept 240-400 kW, leaving megawatt charging in the US confined to heavy-duty vehicles.

insights.claim: Geely's new battery charges at up to 2.2 MW, going from 10 to 70 percent in 4.5 minutes and 10 to 98 percent in 8 minutes 40 seconds, and has been tested in the Zeekr 001 and Lynk and Co 10.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Refuel-parity charging erodes a key EV adoption barrier in China, strengthening Chinese OEMs' competitive edge.

insights.claim: Geely says AI-driven micro current pulses reactivate lithium ions accumulated at the negative electrode during repeated fast charging, extending battery life by 20 percent.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Addresses the main objection (degradation) to routine ultra-fast charging.

insights.claim: CATL leads the race with an LFP battery announced in April that charges 10 to 80 percent in 3 minutes 44 seconds, ahead of BYD's March product at 10 to 70 percent in 5 minutes.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: CATL retains a technology lead in fast-charging LFP, reinforcing its position as the dominant battery supplier.
insights.locator: The numbers eclipse those from BYD

insights.claim: China's EV advantage also stems from deep connected-services integration with an Android phone-maker's update cadence rather than a traditional automaker's.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Software iteration speed is a structural competitive gap for Western automakers.

insights.claim: Most US fast chargers deliver a fraction of Chinese megawatt outputs: most Tesla Superchargers top out at 250 kW, Electrify America at 350 kW, IONNA at 400 kW, and ChargePoint's charger at 600 kW.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: US charging networks face a future upgrade cycle to stay competitive, a capex burden and opportunity for charger hardware makers.
insights.locator: In the US, the most powerful

insights.claim: US-market EVs accept far less power: Hyundai and Kia's 800V EVs max around 240 kW, the Porsche Taycan 320 kW, and newer German EVs like the BMW iX3 and Porsche Cayenne 400 kW.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Vehicle-side limits, not just chargers, keep the US far behind Chinese charge times.

insights.claim: Megawatt charging in the US remains limited to heavy-duty EVs; ChargePoint says pairing two 600 kW Express Solo units on a common DC bus delivers 1.2 MW through one MCS port, beyond what NACS or CCS1 connectors can handle.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Connector standards (NACS/CCS1) cap US passenger-car charge power; MCS is the path to megawatt charging, initially for trucks.
